Yad Malachi Digitization — Pipeline Case Study

Verified Against the Ink

Every correction in this pipeline traces back to a real disagreement, resolved by looking at the actual 1857 page — not inferred, not guessed. Here is what that looks like, word by word.

Method

How we look at a page

The same four-level zoom runs for every one of Part 1's 125 currently-open flagged candidates: a physical page, a paragraph, a bounding box, and finally a structured record. Nothing here is inferred from a clean digital source — there isn't one. It starts as ink on paper.

LEVEL 1

The physical page

Page 76 of the Berlin (~1857) scan, rendered directly from the source PDF. This is all any OCR engine has to work with — a single dense column running the full page width, a running header repeating the work's name, and a printer's letterforms nearly 170 years old.

LEVEL 2

The paragraph

Document AI and the PDF's own text layer each propose a reading for this line. Here the two streams disagree on a single word — the opening of klal 219, האי vs. האו — which is enough to flag the whole token for a closer look.

LEVEL 3

The word, and its box

Every token Document AI extracts carries a bounding box — four numbers, normalized to a 0–1 fraction of the page's width and height, independent of resolution or DPI. That's what lets the pipeline re-crop the exact same spot at 300dpi, years after the original OCR pass ran, and hand a vision model only the pixels in question.

klal 219 · page 76
bbox  x1: 0.7815  y1: 0.6220  x2: 0.8352  y2: 0.6390
LEVEL 4

The structured record

Each flagged token becomes one JSON record: which klal, which page, what the two candidate readings were, the box to re-crop, and — once adjudicated — the model's verdict and confidence.

{
  "klal_id": 219,
  "page": 76,
  "opcode": "replace",
  "original_word": "האי",
  "corrected_word": "האו",
  "bbox": {
    "x1": 0.7815, "y1": 0.6220,
    "x2": 0.8352, "y2": 0.6390
  },
  "vision_selected": "A",
  "vision_confidence": 0.98
}

real record, corrections_verified_part1.json — option A (האי) is the flagged candidate's own original reading; the vision pass confirmed it and rejected the proposed change to האו

The hard case

A boundary, not just a word

The most serious defects aren't misread letters — they're klal boundaries drawn in the wrong place. This is the clearest example on file: klal 82's own closing citation ended up inside klal 83, and no purely semantic read caught it until someone laid the stored text next to the printed page and the raw extraction log.

Here is klal 83's own stored record, exactly as it sat before anyone touched it — this is the actual pre-fix text, not a paraphrase:

פג בשל בשל [.] דף ס"א ב' וש"ות זקן אהרן סי' קפ"ג : תורה הלך אחר המחמיר ובשל סופרים ה הלך אחר המקיל...

the actual pre-fix record, part1.json (git history) — klal_id 83, title field was literally "בשל בשל"

The cause is visible in Document AI's own raw token dump for this exact spot on the page (docai_word_boxes/page_37.json) — every token it extracted, in the order it extracted them, each with its true vertical position on the page (smaller y = higher up):

extracted as token # text y‑position what it is
522ישרא0.7407klal 82's own text — stops here, mid-word
523–524פג בשו0.7772klal 83's gematria + opening word, read once
525בשל0.7676the same word, detected and read a second time
526–536דף ס"א ב' וש"ות זקן אהרן סי' קפ"ג :0.7608klal 82's real citation — physically above both rows before it, extracted after them
537+תורה הלך אחר המחמיר ובשל סופרים...0.7720the rest of klal 83's real opening sentence

Two things are visible in this table at once. Klal 83 opens with a larger, decoratively set first letter — standard for a new klal in this print — and Document AI's layout analysis read that one physical word twice, as two separate tokens (בשו, then בשל). Both duplicates were extracted before the citation line, even though the citation's own y-position (0.7608) sits higher on the page — earlier in true reading order. Whatever stitches the running text together just walks the array in extraction order, so it reproduced both problems at once: a doubled opening word, then a citation that belongs to the klal above, then the real sentence. Untangled, it's one continuous line: בשל תורה הלך אחר המחמיר ובשל סופרים הלך אחר המקיל.

page 37 — klal 82's closing lines running directly into klal 83's opening, as actually printed

klal 82 — correct ending

דף ס״א ב׳ וש״ות זקן אהרן סי׳ קפ״ג

klal 83 — correct opening

פג בשל תורה הלך אחר המחמיר ובשל סופרים הלך אחר המקיל

Read together, the two klalim make a deliberate pair — biblical law leans strict, rabbinic law leans lenient, and klal 82 (בשל סופרים הלך אחר המקיל) is the counterpart klal 83 is built to answer. The scrambled version obscured that relationship entirely, and it's exactly the kind of error a text-only pass tends to miss: the broken version isn't ungrammatical, it's just wrong.

The hidden letter

One glyph, not two letters

The single most consequential defect in the corpus wasn't a misread letter or a misplaced sentence — it was a glyph this print uses that modern OCR has no concept of at all. Finding it took three independent kinds of evidence agreeing, not one confident-looking model output.

Klal 88, page 40. Document AI reads the word here as אא — aleph, aleph, twice in a row. That isn't a word. Here is the actual ink, at 1200dpi:

as OCR read it — "אא"

אא ← page 40, the disputed spot

an ordinary aleph, same line

תנא ← the alef here has no ascender

Look at the left character in the first crop: a tall hooked stroke rises well above the letter body — nothing like the plain aleph on the right, three words away on the same line. That ascender is a ל (lamed). This print sets אל as a single ligature glyph (Unicode U+FB4F); Document AI has no mapping for it, and reads the composite shape as a bare א, silently dropping the lamed. The word isn't אא — it's אלא, "but," one of the commonest words in the Talmudic vocabulary, its two letters fused by a 19th-century typesetter and split apart wrong by a 21st-century model that had never seen this sort before.

page 40, the full line — דשום תנא לא מחייב אלא א"כ הוציאו המצניע זולת רשב"א

One paleographic observation isn't proof by itself — an ascender could be ink bleed, a flaw in this one letterform, a coincidence. Two more signals, independent of the pixels and of each other, had to agree before this became a correction rather than a hunch:

Cross-engine. A second, independently-run OCR pass over this same page reads the identical glyph as a bare לא — keeping the lamed, dropping the aleph instead. Two engines splitting one composite shape in complementary directions is the signature of an unmapped ligature, not two unrelated mistakes.
confirmed
Semantics. Every reconstructed reading is the ordinary, contextually correct word — never a stretch. אינו אלא לא תעשה, קודם אלפא ביתא, בארץ ישראל — real Talmudic phrasing, not a word invented to make the sentence work.
confirmed
Negative control. Klal 44's א״א — a real abbreviation (אשת איש) — shows two plain alefs with a gershayim and no ascender on either. The discrimination is real; it isn't "ascenders everywhere."
confirmed

Once the mechanism was confirmed, it explained a pattern that had been sitting in the corpus for weeks under a different guise — a semantic spot-check had already flagged dozens of sentences that read as slightly-off gibberish, without knowing why. Every affected word turned out to be exactly a word where a ל immediately follows an א: אלא→אא, אליבא→איבא, אלעזר→אעזר, שמואל→שמוא, ישראל→ישרא — the mechanism's fingerprint, not eight unrelated coincidences.

{
  "decision_type": "manual_correction",
  "klal_id": 88,
  "word_index": 383,
  "candidate_snapshot": { "original_word": "אא" },
  "chosen_text": "אלא",
  "note": "Alef-lamed ligature correction ... Individually scan-verified against the ink at 600-1800 DPI."
}

real record, review_decisions.jsonl — one of 131 corrections across 51 klalim this mechanism produced, each recorded through the same flag → human-review → apply pipeline as every other correction in the corpus, never a direct edit.

Adjudication in the record

What the model actually sees

Two more disagreements from the same automated pass, each resolved the same way: crop the exact box, show it to a vision model alongside both candidate readings, and require it to name which one the pixels actually support — never to invent a third option.

klal 21 · page 20confidence 0.98

Reads עורו, not עודו — resh, not dalet.

"Paleographically, the third letter features a smooth rounded shoulder characteristic of a resh, rather than a dalet. Contextually regarding Leviathan (Job 41), 'עורו קשה' ('his hide is tough') is the intended semantic meaning."

klal 218 · page 76confidence 1.00

Reads שגם, not שגס — final mem, not samech.

"Option B contains a typographical error with samech, which does not fit the letterform or the semantic context ('ושאפשר שגם רש״י סובר כן')."

klal 219 · page 76confidence 0.98

Reads האי, not האו — the standard Talmudic idiom.

"Contextually, 'האי תנא דבי ר' ישמעאל' ('this Tanna of the school of R. Ishmael') is a standard Aramaic Talmudic phrase, whereas 'האו' is a transcription error."

Not every fix in the corpus comes from this automated pass. Klal 65's ב״ר→ב״ד correction, for instance, has no entry in the vision-adjudication cache at all — it was caught by direct human cross-reference against the scan and against Mishnah Eduyot 1:5, the ruling the klal actually states. The pipeline keeps that distinction on the record rather than blurring "verified by a person" into "verified by the model": the two are different kinds of evidence, and conflating them is exactly the failure mode the ledger below is trying to avoid.

Assembly

How structure becomes data

Once a klal's text is settled, it collapses into one record — the shape every one of the 667 klalim takes on its way to becoming a Sefaria segment.

{
  "klal_id": 218,
  "gematria": "ריח",
  "section": "כללי ההא",
  "title": "הניחא למ\"ד מופנה מצד אחד למידין ואין משיבין וכו'",
  "clean_text": "ריח הניחא למ\"ד מופנה מצד אחד למידין... שגם רש\"י סובר כן...",
  "page": 30
}

real record, part1.json — one of 222 Part-1 klalim

And every batch of flagged candidates carries its own honesty check built in — a running list of which klalim the pipeline explicitly does not trust yet, so a downstream reviewer never mistakes silence for a clean bill of health:

{
  "total_candidates": 387,
  "klalim_covered": 149,
  "untrusted_klalim_excluded": []
}

real record, corrections_candidates_part1.json — meta block

Where things actually stand

What's proven, and what isn't yet

The method holds up everywhere it's been run rigorously. It hasn't been run everywhere yet — and the difference matters more than the pitch.

Part 1 page-to-klal alignment — the scan-to-text mapping every crop above depends on.
222 / 222 klalim trusted
Part 1 flagged word-level candidates — vision-adjudicated against the actual scan crop.
91 / 125 verified, 90 at ≥0.9 confidence
Parts 2 & 3 (Klalei HaPoskim, Klalei HaDinim — 445 of 667 klalim) — marker-position verification is corpus-wide, and the scan-linkage and vision-adjudication infrastructure has since been built and run over their full page range. It found real, scan-confirmed issues: 916 klalim there carry an open review flag. Not one has been written into the corpus — applying them waits on the same independent confirmation Part 1 is waiting on, by standing decision.

The case

287 dead citations become live links once, and stay that way.

Every example above is a real disagreement, resolved by looking at the actual page — the discipline the rest of the corpus still needs at scale. The harness is built and proven; what's left is running it against the two-thirds of the work it hasn't reached yet.
